questions.q: Which of the following pipelines will display the count of visible (non‑hidden) entries in the current user's home directory?
questions.why: ‘ls $HOME’ lists only non‑hidden items; piping to wc -l counts the lines, giving the number of visible entries.

questions.q: To see the used and available space on the root partition in a human‑readable format, which command should you run?
questions.why: ‘df -h /’ reports filesystem size, used space, and free space for the specified mount point in human‑readable units.

questions.q: In a command synopsis like "ls [options] [files]", what do the square brackets signify?
options: The enclosed items are optional and may be omitted.
The enclosed items are mandatory arguments.
The brackets must be typed literally when entering the command.
The brackets indicate a choice between the listed items.
questions.why: Square brackets in command syntax denote optional components; the user may include or omit them.

questions.q: Which of the following paths is an absolute path in a Linux filesystem?
questions.why: An absolute path starts with a leading slash, so /etc/passwd is absolute; the others are relative.

questions.q: If the current working directory is /home/user/projects, what absolute directory does the relative path ".." refer to?
questions.why: ".." means the parent directory, so from /home/user/projects it resolves to /home/user.

questions.q: What will the command `echo file{1,2,3}.txt` display?
questions.why: Brace expansion creates separate arguments for each comma‑separated element, so the command expands to file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly assigns the value 5 to a variable and then prints it?
questions.why: Variable assignment is done with NAME=value and the value is accessed with a preceding $. The first option follows this syntax.

questions.q: Within a screen session, which key sequence creates a new virtual window?
questions.why: Screen uses the control‑A prefix; pressing Ctrl‑C after it (Ctrl‑A Ctrl‑C) opens a new window.

questions.q: A script must create the full directory tree /var/www/site/data, creating any missing parent directories. Which command will accomplish this in one step?
questions.why: The -p option tells mkdir to create all missing parent directories along the specified path.

questions.q: You need to delete the empty directory hierarchy dir/a/b/c, removing each empty parent directory as well. Which command is appropriate?
questions.why: rmdir -p removes the specified directory and any empty parent directories automatically.

questions.q: To extract human‑readable text strings embedded in a compiled binary file named prog, which utility should you use?
questions.why: The strings command scans a binary file and prints sequences of printable characters.

questions.q: Which command should you use to start Vim with a graphical user interface on a Unix system?
questions.why: The 'gvim' command launches Vim in a new X window, providing a graphical interface.

questions.q: While editing in Vim, which key sequence returns you from insert mode to command mode?
questions.why: Pressing the Escape key exits insert mode and puts Vim back into command mode.

questions.q: A user runs `umask 0002` and then creates a regular file and a directory with the default creation modes. What permission bits will the new file and directory have?
options: rw-r--r-- for the file and rwxr-xr-x for the directory
rw-rw-r-- for the file and rwxrwxr-x for the directory
rw------- for the file and rwx------ for the directory
rwxrwxrwx for the file and rwxrwxrwx for the directory
questions.why: umask 0002 removes write permission for others only, so 666‑0002 = 664 (rw‑rw‑r--) and 777‑0002 = 775 (rwxrwxr-x).

questions.q: Which command will add both the compressed (c) and don’t‑dump (d) attributes to the file `data.txt`?
questions.why: The + operator adds attributes; `+cd` adds both compressed and don’t‑dump to the specified file.

questions.q: Setting the immutable (i) attribute on a file using `chattr` causes which of the following?
options: The file becomes hidden from directory listings
The file is automatically compressed on write
The file can be appended to but not overwritten
The file cannot be altered or removed, even by the root user
questions.why: The immutable attribute prevents any changes or deletion of the file, and this restriction applies to all users, including root.

questions.q: When creating a file name index with updatedb, which option tells the command to begin indexing from a specific directory and continue downward?
questions.why: The -U option specifies a directory from which updatedb should start indexing.

questions.q: Which locate command option makes the search ignore case differences in file names?
questions.why: The -i flag tells locate to perform a case‑insensitive search.

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes the relationship between the 'type' and 'which' commands?
options: 'type' always lists every matching command in the PATH, while 'which' shows only the first.
'type' is a bash builtin and generally runs faster than the external 'which' program.
'type' is an external program located in /usr/bin, while 'which' is a shell builtin.
'which' can locate source code files, whereas 'type' can only find executables.
questions.why: 'type' is built into bash, making it faster than the external 'which' program.

questions.q:
A file contains the following lines:

2.5e2
300
1e3

Which sort command will correctly order these lines numerically, recognizing the scientific notation?
questions.why: The -g option performs a general numeric sort that understands scientific notation such as 2.5e2.

questions.q: You need to compare two directory trees and see differences in all nested subdirectories. Which command will accomplish this?
questions.why: The -r option makes diff recurse into subdirectories, comparing the entire hierarchy.

questions.q: Which diff switch causes the comparison to ignore differences in letter case?
questions.why: The -i flag tells diff to ignore case when comparing text.

questions.q: On a Linux system, the path /dev/sdb3 most likely refers to:
options: A regular text file containing disk usage statistics
A block device representing the third partition on the second SCSI/SATA drive
A network interface for the third Ethernet device
questions.why: /dev/sdb3 is a device file that represents the third partition of the second SCSI/SATA disk (sdb).

questions.q: Which option added to the ps command will cause the output to show a hierarchical view, indenting child processes beneath their parent processes?
questions.why: The -efH flags tell ps to list all processes in full format and display them in a tree (hierarchical) layout.

questions.q: Running the uptime command prints several pieces of information. Which of the following is NOT part of its normal output?
options: The number of users currently logged in
questions.why: Uptime shows time, uptime, user count, and load averages, but it does not report memory usage.

questions.q: In the output generated by the w command, what does the column labeled "JCPU" indicate?
options: The CPU time spent in kernel mode for that user
The total CPU time consumed by all of the user's processes
The CPU time used by processes attached to the user's terminal
The CPU time used by the most recent command the user ran
questions.why: JCPU reports the cumulative CPU time for all processes that are attached to the user's terminal (tty).

questions.q: When an at job is executed, which statement about its environment is correct?
options: The job starts with a completely empty environment.
The job always runs with the root user's environment variables.
The job inherits the current environment variables of the submitting user.
All user-defined aliases are available to the job.
questions.why: The at command preserves the current environment variables but does not include aliases.

questions.q: Which command installs an existing file named "mytasks" as your crontab schedule?
questions.why: Providing a filename without an option tells crontab to install that file as the user's crontab.

questions.q: Which of the following minute‑field specifications is invalid in a crontab entry?
questions.why: A step value of zero (*/0) is not allowed; the divisor must be a positive integer.

questions.q: You are creating a new account and need the user to be a member of the existing groups "audio" and "video" in addition to their primary group. Which useradd option should you use?
options: Use -G with a comma‑separated list of groups
Use -k to specify the group list
Use -g with a comma‑separated list of groups
Use -c to specify the group list
questions.why: The -G option adds the user to supplementary groups listed after it, separated by commas.

questions.q: When running "sudo userdel -r alice", what effect does the -r flag have?
options: It changes the user's default shell to /bin/false
It only deletes the user's mail spool file
It locks the account instead of deleting it
It removes the user's home directory and all its contents
questions.why: The -r option tells userdel to delete the user's home directory and its files along with the account.

questions.q: To rename the login name of an existing user from "bob" to "robert", which usermod option should be used, and what precaution is recommended?
options: Use -c to change the login name, and update the user's home directory afterwards
Use -l to change the login name, and verify that no scripts or services depend on the old name
Use -s to change the login name, and back up /etc/passwd first
Use -d to change the login name, and ensure the new name has a unique UID
questions.why: The -l option changes a user's login name; you should check for dependencies on the old name before renaming.

questions.q: When performing a whois lookup, how can you direct the query to a specific registrar's server?
questions.why: The -h option lets you specify the hostname of the whois server to query.

questions.q: Which ping option limits the number of echo request packets that are sent?
questions.why: The -c N option tells ping to send at most N packets before stopping.

questions.q: Which Lynx command‑line switch causes the program to print the formatted page to standard output and then quit?
questions.why: -dump tells Lynx to output the rendered page to stdout and exit.

questions.q: You started downloading a large file with wget but the connection dropped. Which option should you add to the same wget command to continue the download from where it stopped?
questions.why: -c enables wget’s continue mode, allowing a partially downloaded file to be resumed.

questions.q: Which printf format string will display a floating‑point number in a field eight characters wide, padded with leading zeros, and showing exactly two digits after the decimal point?
questions.why: The 0 flag adds leading zeros, 8 sets the minimum width, and .2 specifies two digits after the decimal point.

questions.q: You need to run a script called install.sh that asks for confirmation repeatedly. Which command will automatically supply a "yes" answer to every prompt?
questions.why: The yes command writes "y" repeatedly to its standard output, which can be piped into the script’s standard input.

questions.q: In the command wc -l notes.txt, what is -l?
options: An argument naming the file to read
An option that changes how the program behaves
questions.why: Options usually start with a dash and modify the program; here -l makes wc count lines. notes.txt is the argument and wc is the program.

questions.q: Which command is the same as wc -l -w file?
questions.why: Most programs accept single-letter options combined after one dash, so -lw equals -l -w. A few quirky programs don't support combining.

questions.q: What is the default shell for user accounts on most Linux distributions?
questions.why: bash, the Bourne-Again Shell, is the usual default. Other shells such as ksh and csh exist and share most basic features.

questions.q: Which file under /proc shows information about the system's processors?
questions.why: /proc/cpuinfo lists each CPU's model, speed and flags. /proc/version shows the kernel version and /proc/uptime the seconds since boot.

questions.q: What does /proc/self point to?
options: Information about the process reading it
questions.why: /proc/self is a symbolic link to /proc/<PID> of whichever process accesses it, so it changes every time a new command reads it.

questions.q: Which command prints the same kernel information as /proc/version?
questions.why: uname prints kernel name, release and version. uptime shows how long the system has run.

questions.q: Which operator sends a command's standard output to a file, replacing anything already in it?
questions.why: > creates or overwrites the file. >> appends, < reads standard input from a file and 2> redirects standard error.

questions.q: How do you append a command's output to the end of an existing file?
questions.why: >> adds to the end of the file instead of overwriting it, creating the file if it doesn't exist.

questions.q: How do you redirect only the error messages of a command to a file?
questions.why: File descriptor 2 is standard error. 2> sends it to the file while normal output still goes to the screen.

questions.q: Which redirects both standard output and standard error into a single file in bash?
questions.why: &> (or >& file, or > file 2>&1) sends both streams to the same file.

questions.q: What does the pipe in who | sort do?
options: Runs who and sort at random
Saves who's output to a file called sort
Sends who's output to sort as its input
Runs sort only if who fails
questions.why: The pipe connects one program's standard output to the next program's standard input, so sort receives the list of logged-in users.

questions.q: A long cat command is scrolling past. Which keystroke usually stops it?
questions.why: Ctrl+C sends an interrupt that ends the foreground program. Ctrl+Z suspends it and Ctrl+D sends end-of-file.

questions.q: How do you bring background job number 1 back to the foreground?
questions.why: fg resumes a job in the foreground. bg resumes a stopped job in the background and jobs lists them.

questions.q: After killing a program, your terminal no longer shows what you type. Which command usually restores it?
questions.why: reset reinitialises the terminal. Type it blind and press Ctrl+J (a newline) if Enter isn't working.

questions.q: Which cat option numbers every line of output?
questions.why: -n numbers all lines and -b numbers only non-blank ones. -s squeezes repeated blank lines and -E shows $ at line ends.

questions.q: Which command shows a text file one screen at a time and lets you scroll back?
questions.why: less is a pager that lets you scroll up and down and search with /. cat prints everything at once.

questions.q: In vim, which keys save the file and quit?
questions.why: :wq writes and quits. :q! quits without saving, and ZZ (not ZQ) also saves and quits.

questions.q: In vim, how do you leave insert mode?
questions.why: vim is modal: i enters insert mode for typing, and Esc returns to normal (command) mode.

questions.q: What does the sticky bit do when set on a directory such as /tmp?
options: Only a file's owner (or root) can delete or rename files in it
New files inherit the directory's group
Files in it run with the owner's privileges
questions.why: Normally write permission on a directory lets you delete any file in it. With the sticky bit, users can only remove their own files.

questions.q: With a umask of 0022, what permissions does a newly created regular file get?
questions.why: Files start from 0666 and the umask removes bits: 0666 minus 0022 leaves 0644. Directories start at 0777 and would get 0755.

questions.q: With a umask of 0002, what permission does a new directory get?
questions.why: Directories start from 0777; removing the 0002 bit (other-write) gives 0775, rwxrwxr-x.

questions.q: Why use find -print0 | xargs -0 instead of find -print | xargs?
options: It runs faster on large disks
It handles filenames that contain spaces correctly
questions.why: -print0 separates names with null characters and xargs -0 splits on them, so a file called my stuff isn't split into two arguments.

questions.q: Which xargs option runs the command once per input line?
questions.why: -n1 passes one argument to each run of the command. -0 changes the delimiter and -p asks before each run.

questions.q: Which command joins files side by side as columns?
questions.why: paste combines lines from several files into columns, separated by tabs by default. cut does the opposite and extracts columns.

questions.q: Which cut option sets the field delimiter?
questions.why: -d sets the delimiter character (tab by default) and -f picks the field numbers, as in cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd.

questions.q: Which command translates or deletes characters, for example converting lower case to upper case?
questions.why: tr maps one set of characters to another: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'. With -d it deletes characters.

questions.q: Which tar option creates a new archive?
questions.why: -c creates, -x extracts, -t lists the contents and -r appends files to an existing archive.

questions.q: What does tar -tzf backup.tar.gz do?
options: Tests the archive for errors and repairs it
Lists the contents of a gzip-compressed archive
questions.why: -t lists, -z handles gzip compression and -f names the archive file.

questions.q: Which tar option uses bzip2 compression?
questions.why: -j is bzip2, -z is gzip and -J is xz. -Z was old Unix compress.

questions.q: Which command creates a SHA-256 checksum of a file?
questions.why: SHA-256 is far more reliable than the old sum and cksum programs; md5sum works but MD5 is weak.

questions.q: How do you check files against a saved list of checksums?
questions.why: --check (-c) reads the saved sums, recomputes them and prints OK or FAILED for each file.

questions.q: When you run mount /usr with no device named, where does mount look up what to mount?
questions.why: mount reads /etc/fstab to find the device, filesystem type and options for that mount point.

questions.q: Which mount option mounts every filesystem listed in /etc/fstab?
questions.why: mount -a mounts all fstab entries except those marked noauto. It's also a good test that new fstab lines are valid.

questions.q: Why should you unmount a USB drive before removing it?
options: So cached writes are flushed and the filesystem is left consistent
questions.why: Linux caches writes. umount flushes them and marks the filesystem clean, so pulling the drive doesn't lose or corrupt data.

questions.q: Which command interactively shows the most active processes and refreshes every few seconds?
questions.why: top updates in place and lets you sort, renice and kill. ps shows a one-time snapshot.

questions.q: Which command schedules a one-time job, for example at 07:00 tomorrow?
questions.why: at runs a job once at the given time; atq lists queued jobs and atrm removes one. crontab is for recurring jobs.

questions.q: Which command edits your crontab?
questions.why: crontab -e opens your crontab in your editor and installs it on save. -l lists it and -r deletes it.

questions.q: How often does cron check for jobs that are due?
questions.why: The cron daemon wakes every minute, reads the crontabs and runs any job whose time matches.

questions.q: Which useradd option adds a user to extra groups?
questions.why: -G lists supplementary groups. -g sets the primary group, -m creates the home directory and -c sets the comment (full name).

questions.q: What does useradd -m do?
options: Creates the home directory and copies files from /etc/skel
questions.why: -m creates /home/<user> and copies the skeleton files such as .bashrc from /etc/skel.

questions.q: Which command deletes user smith and also removes the home directory?
questions.why: userdel alone leaves the home directory. -r removes it and the mail spool too.

questions.q: How do you lock a user account without deleting it?
questions.why: usermod -L puts a ! in front of the password hash so password logins fail, while files and the account remain.

questions.q: Which command shows the IP addresses on every interface?
questions.why: ip addr lists addresses per interface. ip route shows the routing table and ip link shows link-layer settings.

questions.q: Which command shows the routing table?
questions.why: ip route (ip r) lists destinations and gateways, including the default route.

questions.q: Which older command is the ancestor of ip and is now considered obsolete on many systems?
questions.why: ifconfig from net-tools still exists on many systems but ip from iproute2 replaces it and does much more.

questions.q: Which shell loop runs until its condition becomes true?
questions.why: until repeats while the test command returns non-zero (false) and stops when it succeeds. while is the opposite.

questions.q: What prints the numbers 1 to 5 in a bash for loop?
options: for i in $(seq 1 5); do echo $i; done
questions.why: seq generates the list and command substitution hands it to for. {1..5} brace expansion also works in bash.

questions.q: Which directory holds system-wide configuration files?
questions.why: /etc holds configuration as readable text, such as /etc/fstab and /etc/passwd. /var holds variable data like logs.

questions.q: What is in the /boot directory?
options: The kernel, initial RAM disk and boot loader files
questions.why: /boot contains vmlinuz (the kernel), the initramfs and GRUB's configuration.

questions.q: What does /dev contain?
options: Device nodes for the hardware the kernel knows about
questions.why: Following the everything-is-a-file idea, devices such as disks appear as files like /dev/sda.

questions.q: When you delete a symbolic link with rm, what is removed?
options: Only the link; the target stays
Both the link and the target
questions.why: Most operations follow a link to its target, but rm removes the link itself and leaves the file it points to.

questions.q: Which command removes a directory and everything inside it?
questions.why: rm -r recurses into subdirectories. rmdir only removes an empty directory.

questions.q: Which command removes duplicate adjacent lines, usually after sort?
questions.why: uniq drops repeated adjacent lines, so the input must be sorted first. uniq -d shows only the duplicates.

questions.q: What does wc print with no options?
questions.why: wc reports three counts: lines, words and bytes. -l, -w and -c select one.

questions.q: Where does bash keep your command history by default?
questions.why: bash writes the session's history to ~/.bash_history when you exit; history shows the list.

questions.q: Which command searches your history for previous commands that contained /usr/bin?
questions.why: Piping history into grep filters it; !88 would then re-run entry 88.

questions.q: Which command changes a file's owner to bob and its group to users?
questions.why: chown owner:group sets both. chown :group changes only the group, and chown bob: also sets bob's login group.

questions.q: Who can use chown to give a file to another user?
options: Any member of the file's group
questions.why: Giving away files is restricted to root so users can't dodge quotas or plant files as someone else.

questions.q: What does export do in bash?
options: Makes a variable available to programs started from the shell
questions.why: Exported variables become environment variables that child processes inherit; unexported ones stay in the shell.

questions.q: Which command prints the environment variables?
questions.why: printenv lists environment variables. set also shows shell variables and functions.

questions.q: In vi, which key opens a new line below the cursor and enters insert mode?
questions.why: o opens a line below and O opens one above; both switch to insert mode.

questions.q: In vi, what does dd do?
questions.why: d plus a movement deletes text; dd deletes the whole line and 5dd deletes five lines. x deletes one character.

questions.q: In vi, how do you undo the last change?
questions.why: u undoes the last change in normal mode. Ctrl+Z suspends the editor instead.

questions.q: Which file do you edit to make a custom PS1 prompt permanent for your user?
questions.why: ~/.bashrc runs for each interactive shell, so setting and exporting PS1 there keeps the prompt.

questions.q: What decides most of a distribution's quality according to experienced users, more than its desktop look?
questions.why: Software changes constantly, so how packages are managed and how active support is matters most day to day.

questions.q: Before running fdisk on a USB drive, what should you do?
questions.why: Partitioning a mounted device risks corruption, so umount /dev/sdb1 first, then run fdisk on the whole device, /dev/sdb.

questions.q: In fdisk, which command adds a new partition?
questions.why: n creates a partition, d deletes one, p prints the table and w writes changes and exits.

questions.q: What does fdisk's q command do?
questions.why: Nothing is written until w. q leaves without changing the disk.

questions.q: What does ssh warn you about when a server's host key has changed?
options: The remote host's identity may have changed, possibly an attack
questions.why: ssh stores host keys in known_hosts. A changed key could mean a reinstall, or someone intercepting the connection.

questions.q: How do you log in to a remote system as a different user, bob?
questions.why: user@host tells ssh which account to use; ssh -l bob remote-sys works too.

questions.q: Which command shows all of a file's timestamps, inode and permissions?
questions.why: stat shows access, modify and change times, inode number, links and permissions in detail.

questions.q: What does touch do to an existing file?
questions.why: touch sets the access and modification times to the current time; on a missing file it creates an empty one.

questions.q: What does rsync --delete do?
options: Deletes files older than a week
Removes files at the destination that no longer exist at the source
questions.why: --delete makes the destination an exact mirror of the source, which is useful for backups but dangerous if paths are wrong.

questions.q: What does the r in rsync stand for?
questions.why: rsync can copy over a network via ssh, transferring only the differences between files.

questions.q: Which locate option enables extended regular expressions?
questions.why: --regex uses extended regular expressions and --regexp uses basic ones.

questions.q: In less, how do you search forward for a pattern?
questions.why: /pattern searches forward and n jumps to the next match. ? searches backward.

questions.q: Which diff option produces the unified format used by patches?
questions.why: -u gives unified output with + and - lines. -c is the context format and -q only says whether files differ.

questions.q: In default diff output, what does 1d0 mean?
options: Line 1 of the first file must be deleted
questions.why: Default diff uses commands such as a (append), c (change) and d (delete) to turn the first file into the second.

questions.q: What does the nl command do?
questions.why: nl numbers lines, by default only non-blank ones (-b t). -b a numbers all lines.

questions.q: Why are terminals traditionally 80 characters wide?
options: Printers printed about 80 characters across a page
questions.why: At 10 characters per inch on letter paper, with margins, 80 characters was the widest print line.

questions.q: In a makefile, what does CC= gcc set?
questions.why: Variables like CC are substituted later, so $(CC) becomes gcc when make runs.

questions.q: What is top-down design?
options: Breaking a large task into steps, then each step into smaller ones
Writing code from the last line up
Testing a program before writing it
questions.why: Top-down design keeps refining high-level steps into small tasks, which suits shell scripts built from functions.

questions.q: What does [ -d temp ] || exit 1 do in a script?
options: Exits with status 1 if the directory temp doesn't exist
questions.why: || runs the second command only if the first fails, so a missing temp directory ends the script.

questions.q: What does id -u print?
options: The numeric user ID of the effective user
questions.why: id -u prints the UID; root is always 0, so scripts compare it with 0 to check for superuser rights.

questions.q: Why can [ $number = 1 ] fail with 'unary operator expected'?
options: If number is empty, the test becomes [ = 1 ]
questions.why: An empty variable vanishes on expansion. Quoting it, [ "$number" = 1 ], keeps an empty string in place.

questions.q: What is the general rule for quoting variables in shell scripts?
options: Double-quote variables and command substitutions unless you want word splitting
questions.why: Double quotes stop empty values from vanishing and names with spaces from splitting into several words.

questions.q: In a script's option loop, what does shift do?
options: Moves the positional parameters left so $2 becomes $1
Runs the next command in the background
questions.why: shift drops $1 and moves the rest down, so a while loop can process arguments one at a time until none remain.

questions.q: What does read -p "Name: " name do?
options: Shows a prompt and stores the user's input in name
questions.why: read takes a line from standard input; -p prints a prompt first.

questions.q: In bash arithmetic, what does (( 0 )) return as an exit status?
questions.why: (( )) maps arithmetic results to exit codes: a non-zero result is success (0) and zero is failure (1).

questions.q: Why give temporary files unpredictable names?
options: To prevent temp race attacks in shared /tmp
questions.why: If an attacker can guess the name, they can create it first as a link to something sensitive. mktemp makes safe names.

questions.q: Which command creates a temporary file with a random, safe name?
questions.why: mktemp replaces the X characters in its template with random letters and creates the file securely.

questions.q: Which command lists block devices such as disks and partitions in a tree?
questions.why: lsblk shows disks, partitions and their mount points. lsmod lists kernel modules and lsof open files.

questions.q: Which command shows how much space is free on each mounted filesystem?
questions.why: df reports filesystem usage; -h prints sizes in human-readable units. du measures directory sizes instead.

questions.q: Which command shows the total size of a directory?
questions.why: du -s summarises the total and -h makes it readable, such as 1.2G.

questions.q: Which command shows memory and swap usage?
questions.why: free shows total, used and available RAM and swap; -h uses human-readable units.

questions.q: Which ps command lists every process on the system with full details?
questions.why: ps aux shows all users' processes with CPU, memory and command line. Plain ps shows only your terminal's processes.

questions.q: Which signal does kill send by default?
questions.why: SIGTERM asks the process to exit cleanly. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which can't be caught, so use it only as a last resort.

questions.q: Which command runs a program with a lower scheduling priority?
questions.why: nice starts a command with an adjusted niceness; higher values mean lower priority. renice changes a running process.

questions.q: Which command keeps a program running after you log out?
questions.why: nohup ignores the hangup signal sent at logout, and & puts the job in the background.

questions.q: Which grep option searches recursively through directories?
questions.why: -r recurses. -i ignores case, -v inverts the match and -c counts matching lines.

questions.q: Which grep option shows lines that do not match the pattern?
questions.why: -v inverts the match. -l lists only file names and -n adds line numbers.

questions.q: Which command finds files under /home larger than 100 MB?
questions.why: find tests attributes; -size +100M means more than 100 megabytes.

questions.q: Which find test finds files modified within the last day?
questions.why: -mtime -1 means modified less than one day ago; +1 means more than one day ago.

questions.q: Which command changes a file so its owner can read, write and execute and no one else has any access?
questions.why: 7 is rwx for the owner and 0 removes everything for group and others. 600 would give rw without execute.

questions.q: What does chmod u+x script.sh do?
options: Adds execute permission for the file's owner
Makes the script run as root
questions.why: Symbolic mode: u is the user who owns the file, + adds and x is execute.

questions.q: Which line at the top of a script tells the system to run it with bash?
questions.why: The shebang (#!) names the interpreter the kernel should use when the file is run directly.

questions.q: Which variable holds the exit status of the last command?
questions.why: $? is 0 for success and non-zero for failure. $$ is the shell's PID, $! the last background PID and $# the argument count.

questions.q: Which variable holds the number of arguments passed to a script?
questions.why: $# counts the positional parameters. $@ and $* expand to the arguments themselves and $0 is the script name.

questions.q: Which command makes ls -la available as ll for the current session?
questions.why: alias defines a shortcut; put it in ~/.bashrc to keep it across sessions.

questions.q: Which command shows where a command's executable is in your PATH?
questions.why: which searches PATH and prints the first matching executable. type also tells you if it's an alias or builtin.

questions.q: Which command displays the manual page for a command?
questions.why: man shows the manual. For bash builtins, help gives built-in documentation.

questions.q: Which archive command compresses a file, replacing it with file.gz?
questions.why: gzip compresses in place and removes the original; gunzip reverses it and zcat prints the content without decompressing to disk.

questions.q: Which command copies a directory and its contents?
questions.why: cp needs -r (or -a to preserve attributes) to copy directories recursively.

questions.q: What does ln -s target linkname create?
questions.why: -s makes a symbolic (soft) link, a pointer to a path. Without -s, ln creates a hard link to the same inode.

questions.q: What is a difference between hard links and symbolic links?
options: A symlink keeps the data if the target is deleted
Hard links can point to directories freely
A hard link can't span filesystems; a symlink can
questions.why: Hard links are extra names for the same inode on one filesystem. Symlinks store a path, which can be anywhere but breaks if the target goes.

questions.q: Which command shows the last 20 lines of a log and keeps printing new lines as they arrive?
questions.why: tail -f follows the file as it grows, which is how admins watch logs live.

questions.q: Which sort option sorts numerically rather than alphabetically?
questions.why: -n compares numbers, so 10 comes after 9. -r reverses, -u removes duplicates and -k picks a field.

questions.q: Which command prints the current working directory?
questions.why: pwd shows the full path of the directory you're in.

questions.q: What does cd with no arguments do?
questions.why: cd on its own, like cd ~, takes you to your home directory.

questions.q: What does cd - do?
questions.why: The shell keeps the last directory in OLDPWD and cd - switches back to it.

questions.q: Which ls option shows hidden files?
questions.why: Files whose names start with a dot are hidden unless you use -a.

questions.q: Which ls option lists files in long format with permissions and sizes?
questions.why: Long format shows type, permissions, links, owner, group, size and date.

questions.q: Which ls option sorts by modification time, newest first?
questions.why: -t sorts by time; add -r to reverse the order.

questions.q: Which ls option sorts by file size?
questions.why: -S lists largest first; -s just shows block sizes next to names.

questions.q: What does the first character d mean in ls -l output?
questions.why: - is a regular file, d a directory, l a symbolic link.

questions.q: What does an l at the start of ls -l output mean?
options: The entry is a symbolic link
questions.why: Symlinks show their target after an arrow, such as link -> target.

questions.q: What does the wildcard * match?
options: Any number of characters, including none
questions.why: *.txt matches every file ending in .txt.

questions.q: What does [abc] match in a filename pattern?
options: Any one of the characters a, b or c
questions.why: Brackets match a single character from the set.

questions.q: What does mv old.txt new.txt do?
questions.why: mv renames within a filesystem, or moves files between directories.

questions.q: What does cp -i do?
options: Asks before overwriting an existing file
questions.why: -i (interactive) prevents accidentally overwriting files.

questions.q: What does cp -a preserve?
options: Permissions, ownership, timestamps and links, copying recursively
questions.why: -a (archive) makes an exact copy, useful for backups.

questions.q: What does rm -i do?
options: Asks for confirmation before deleting each file
questions.why: Interactive mode helps avoid deleting the wrong files.

questions.q: Why is rm -rf dangerous?
options: It deletes recursively and forcefully without asking, with no undo
questions.why: A typo in the path can wipe large parts of a system.

questions.q: What does mkdir -p a/b/c do?
options: Creates a, a/b and a/b/c as needed
questions.why: -p creates missing parents and doesn't error if they exist.

questions.q: What does the file command do?
options: Identifies a file's type by examining its contents
questions.why: file tells you whether something is text, an image, an executable and so on.

questions.q: What does head -n 5 file do?
questions.why: head shows the start of a file; tail shows the end.

questions.q: What does tail -f do?
options: Keeps showing new lines as they are added to a file
questions.why: Following a log in real time is a common use.

questions.q: Which command concatenates files and prints them?
questions.why: cat file1 file2 prints both in order; tac prints lines in reverse.

questions.q: Which command searches for text inside files?
questions.why: grep prints lines matching a pattern; find searches for files by attributes.

questions.q: Which grep option ignores case?
questions.why: -i makes Error, ERROR and error all match.

questions.q: Which grep option shows line numbers with matches?
questions.why: -n helps locate matches inside large files.

questions.q: Which grep option prints only the names of files containing a match?
questions.why: -l lists matching files without the matching lines.

questions.q: Which grep option counts matching lines?
questions.why: -c prints a count per file instead of the lines.

questions.q: Which grep option matches whole words only?
questions.why: grep -w cat matches the word cat but not concatenate.

questions.q: What does grep -o do?
options: Prints only the matching part of each line
questions.why: -o is handy for extracting things like IP addresses.

questions.q: Which command finds files by name under /etc?
questions.why: find searches the live filesystem; locate uses a prebuilt database.

questions.q: Which find option matches only regular files?
questions.why: -type d matches directories and -type l symbolic links.

questions.q: How does find run a command on each file it finds?
questions.why: {} is replaced by each file name and \; ends the command.

questions.q: Which find test matches files owned by a specific user?
questions.why: find / -user alice lists files alice owns.

questions.q: Which find test matches files with exactly permissions 644?
questions.why: -perm -644 means at least those bits; -perm 644 means exactly.

questions.q: What is the advantage of locate over find?
options: It's much faster because it searches a database
questions.why: The database may be out of date until updatedb runs.

questions.q: Which command updates the locate database?
questions.why: updatedb usually runs daily from cron; run it manually to include new files.

questions.q: What does which ls show?
options: The path of the ls program that would run
questions.why: which searches PATH for the first matching executable.

questions.q: What does type cd tell you?
options: That cd is a shell builtin
questions.why: type identifies builtins, aliases, functions and files.

questions.q: What does whatis do?
options: Shows a one-line description of a command
questions.why: whatis ls prints the short NAME line from its man page.

questions.q: What does apropos do?
options: Searches man page descriptions for a keyword
questions.why: apropos network finds commands related to networking.

questions.q: Which man section contains user commands?
questions.why: Section 5 is file formats and section 8 is admin commands.

questions.q: How do you view the man page for the passwd file format rather than the command?
questions.why: Specifying section 5 picks the file format page.

questions.q: Which section of the manual holds system administration commands?
questions.why: Commands like useradd and mount are documented in section 8.

questions.q: What are the three permission classes in Linux?
questions.why: Each class gets its own read, write and execute bits.

questions.q: What does execute permission on a directory allow?
options: Running the directory as a program
Entering the directory and accessing files in it
questions.why: Read lists names; execute lets you cd into it and reach files.

questions.q: What does write permission on a directory allow?
options: Creating, deleting and renaming files in it
questions.why: Deleting a file depends on the directory's permissions, not the file's.

questions.q: What is the numeric value of rwx?
questions.why: r=4, w=2, x=1, so rwx is 7, rw- is 6 and r-x is 5.

questions.q: What permissions does chmod 640 file set?
options: rw- for owner, r-- for group, none for others
questions.why: 6 is rw for the owner, 4 is r for the group, and 0 gives others nothing.

questions.q: What does chmod g+w file do?
options: Adds write permission for the group
questions.why: Symbolic mode uses u, g, o and a with +, - or =.

questions.q: What does chmod o-r file do?
questions.why: o means others, users who aren't the owner or in the group.

questions.q: What does chmod -R do?
options: Applies the change recursively to a directory and its contents
questions.why: Be careful: execute bits applied to every file may not be wanted.

questions.q: What is the setuid bit?
options: A program runs with its owner's privileges rather than the user's
questions.why: passwd uses setuid root so users can update /etc/shadow.

questions.q: How does setuid appear in ls -l output?
options: A capital S at the start
An s in place of the owner's x
questions.why: rwsr-xr-x shows setuid on an executable.

questions.q: What does the setgid bit do on a directory?
options: Only the owner can list it
New files inherit the directory's group
questions.why: It's handy for shared project directories.

questions.q: How does the sticky bit appear on /tmp in ls -l?
options: An s in the owner's x
A capital T at the start
A t in place of others' x
questions.why: drwxrwxrwt shows the sticky bit as a t in the others' execute position.

questions.q: Which command changes a file's group only?
questions.why: chgrp staff file sets the group; chown :staff file does the same.

questions.q: What does a + at the end of ls -l permissions mean?
options: The file has an access control list
questions.why: The + means extra ACL entries exist; getfacl shows them.

questions.q: Which command shows a file's ACL?
questions.why: setfacl changes ACLs; getfacl displays them.

questions.q: Which command shows extended attributes such as immutable?
questions.why: chattr +i sets immutable, and lsattr shows it.

questions.q: What does sudo do?
options: Runs a command with another user's privileges, usually root
questions.why: Access is controlled by /etc/sudoers and is logged.

questions.q: How should /etc/sudoers be edited?
options: With visudo, which checks the syntax before saving
questions.why: A syntax error in sudoers could lock everyone out of sudo.

questions.q: What does su - do?
options: Switches to root with a full login environment
questions.why: The dash loads the target user's environment, as if they logged in.

questions.q: What does the id command show?
options: Your user ID, group ID and groups
questions.why: id alice shows another user's IDs and groups.

questions.q: What does whoami show?
questions.why: Useful after su or sudo to confirm who you are.

questions.q: What does the who command show?
questions.why: w shows the same with what each user is doing.

questions.q: Which file stores group definitions?
questions.why: /etc/group lists group names, GIDs and members.

questions.q: Which command creates a group?
questions.why: groupadd -g 3000 devs creates a group with a chosen GID.

questions.q: Which command adds an existing user to a supplementary group without removing others?
questions.why: Without -a, -G replaces the user's supplementary groups.

questions.q: Which command changes a user's password?
questions.why: Root can run passwd username to set another user's password.

questions.q: Which command shows password ageing for a user?
questions.why: chage -l lists expiry and last-change dates.

questions.q: What does a login shell of /sbin/nologin do?
options: Prevents interactive logins for that account
questions.why: Service accounts often use it so nobody can log in as them.

questions.q: What is the root user's UID?
questions.why: Any account with UID 0 has full superuser rights.

questions.q: What does ps -ef show?
questions.why: -e selects all processes and -f adds details like the parent PID.

questions.q: What is a PID?
questions.why: Every running process gets a unique process ID that commands like kill use.

questions.q: What is a zombie process?
options: A process that has finished but whose parent hasn't collected its exit status
questions.why: Zombies use almost no resources; many usually mean a buggy parent.

questions.q: What does kill -9 PID send?
options: SIGKILL, which can't be caught or ignored
questions.why: Use SIGTERM first so the program can clean up.

questions.q: What does SIGHUP often tell a daemon to do?
questions.why: Many services re-read their config files on SIGHUP.

questions.q: Which command kills processes by name?
questions.why: pkill httpd signals all processes whose names match.

questions.q: What does pgrep sshd do?
options: Prints the PIDs of processes named sshd
questions.why: pgrep -a also shows the full command line.

questions.q: What does the & at the end of a command do?
questions.why: The shell prints a job number and PID and gives you the prompt back.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+Z do to a running foreground job?
options: Sends it to the background running
questions.why: Use bg to resume it in the background or fg in the foreground.

questions.q: What does the jobs command list?
options: Jobs started from the current shell
questions.why: Each job has a number like %1 for fg, bg and kill.

questions.q: What does nice -n 19 command do?
options: Runs it with the lowest scheduling priority
Runs it with the highest priority
questions.why: Niceness ranges from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest).

questions.q: Who can set a negative nice value?
questions.why: Ordinary users can only make their processes nicer, not more aggressive.

questions.q: What does uptime show?
options: Current time, how long the system has run, users and load averages
questions.why: The three load averages cover 1, 5 and 15 minutes.

questions.q: What does a load average higher than the number of CPU cores suggest?
options: Processes are waiting for CPU time
questions.why: Sustained high load means the system is overloaded.

questions.q: What does free -h show?
options: Memory and swap usage in readable units
questions.why: Look at the available column, not just free, for usable memory.

questions.q: What is swap space?
options: Disk space used as overflow when RAM is full
questions.why: Heavy swapping slows a system because disks are much slower than RAM.

questions.q: What does df -i show?
questions.why: A filesystem can run out of inodes even with free space if it has many small files.

questions.q: What does du -sh * do in a directory?
options: Shows the size of each item in the directory
questions.why: It quickly reveals which subdirectory uses the most space.

questions.q: What is a mount point?
options: A directory where a filesystem is attached to the tree
questions.why: Mounting /dev/sdb1 on /data makes its contents appear under /data.

questions.q: What does findmnt show?
options: Mounted filesystems in a tree, with sources and options
questions.why: findmnt /data quickly confirms what's mounted there.

questions.q: What does blkid show?
options: Block devices with their UUIDs, labels and filesystem types
questions.why: UUIDs from blkid are the safest way to reference disks in fstab.

questions.q: Why use UUIDs instead of device names like /dev/sdb1 in /etc/fstab?
options: Device names can change between boots; UUIDs don't
questions.why: Adding a disk can renumber /dev/sdX names.

questions.q: What are the six fields of an /etc/fstab line?
options: Source, target, port, protocol, action, log
User, group, mode, size, date, name
Device, mount point, filesystem type, options, dump, fsck order
IP, mask, gateway, DNS, hostname, domain
questions.why: For example: UUID=... /data xfs defaults 0 0.

questions.q: Which command creates an ext4 filesystem on /dev/sdb1?
questions.why: mkfs builds a filesystem; fdisk only partitions.

questions.q: Which command checks and repairs an unmounted ext4 filesystem?
questions.why: Never run fsck on a mounted filesystem; XFS uses xfs_repair.

questions.q: Which command lists partitions on all disks?
questions.why: lsblk shows a tree of disks and partitions.

questions.q: What is the difference between MBR and GPT partition tables?
options: GPT works only on USB drives
GPT supports larger disks and many more partitions
questions.why: MBR is limited to 2 TB and four primary partitions.

questions.q: What does LVM add over plain partitions?
options: Flexible volumes that can be resized and span multiple disks
questions.why: Physical volumes form volume groups, which are carved into logical volumes.

questions.q: What is the order of LVM building blocks from disk up?
options: Volume group, physical volume, logical volume
Physical volume, volume group, logical volume
Logical volume, volume group, physical volume
questions.why: pvcreate, vgcreate and lvcreate build them in that order.

questions.q: What does tar -xzf archive.tar.gz -C /tmp do?
questions.why: -C changes to a directory before extracting.

questions.q: What does zip -r archive.zip dir do?
options: Creates a zip archive of a directory recursively
questions.why: -r includes subdirectories; unzip archive.zip extracts it again.

questions.q: What does gunzip file.gz do?
questions.why: gunzip restores the original file and removes the .gz; gzip -d does the same.

questions.q: Which compression tool generally gives the best compression ratio of these?
questions.why: xz is slower but produces smaller files than gzip or bzip2.

questions.q: What does sort -u do?
questions.why: It's equivalent to sort | uniq for removing duplicates.

questions.q: What does sort -k2 do?
questions.why: Combine with -t to set the field separator, such as -t,.

questions.q: What does sort -r do?
questions.why: sort -rn sorts numbers from largest to smallest.

questions.q: What does tee do?
options: Writes input to a file and also passes it on to standard output
questions.why: command | tee log.txt saves output while still showing it.

questions.q: What does sed 's/old/new/g' file do?
options: Replaces every occurrence of old with new on each line and prints the result
questions.why: Without g, only the first match on each line is replaced; -i edits in place.

questions.q: What does awk '{print $1}' file do?
options: Prints the first field of each line
questions.why: awk splits lines on whitespace by default.

questions.q: How do you make awk use a colon as the field separator?
questions.why: -F sets the field separator, so -F: splits /etc/passwd into its fields.

questions.q: What does diff file1 file2 show?
questions.why: No output means the files are identical.

questions.q: What does cmp do?
options: Compares two files byte by byte and reports the first difference
questions.why: cmp reports the first differing byte, which makes it useful for binary files.

questions.q: Which command shows the differences between two directories?
questions.why: diff -r recurses into subdirectories and compares every file it finds.

questions.q: What is an environment variable?
options: A named value the shell passes to programs it starts
questions.why: Programs inherit them from the shell; examples include PATH, HOME and LANG.

questions.q: What does the PATH variable do?
options: Lists the directories the shell searches for commands
questions.why: Commands outside PATH need a full or relative path to run.

questions.q: How do you run a script in the current directory that isn't in PATH?
questions.why: The current directory isn't in PATH by default for safety.

questions.q: What does echo $HOME print?
questions.why: The $ makes the shell expand the variable, so you see the path, not the word.

questions.q: What is the difference between single and double quotes in bash?
options: Double quotes allow variable expansion; single quotes keep text literal
questions.why: echo '$HOME' prints $HOME; echo "$HOME" prints the path.

questions.q: What is command substitution?
options: Replacing a command with an alias
Running a command and inserting its output, as in $(date)
questions.why: today=$(date +%F) stores the date in a variable.

questions.q: What does ~/.bash_profile usually do?
questions.why: Many setups source ~/.bashrc from it so settings apply everywhere.

questions.q: What is /etc/profile?
options: System-wide startup settings for login shells
questions.why: Settings there apply to every user's login shell.

questions.q: What does source ~/.bashrc do?
options: Runs the file in the current shell so changes take effect now
questions.why: The dot command, . ~/.bashrc, does the same.

questions.q: What does history -c do?
options: Clears the current session's command history
questions.why: Without writing, ~/.bash_history may still hold earlier entries.

questions.q: What does !! do in bash?
questions.why: sudo !! reruns the last command with sudo.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+R do in bash?
questions.why: Type part of a command to find it, then Enter to run it.

questions.q: What does Tab do at the bash prompt?
questions.why: Pressing it twice lists the possible completions.

questions.q: What is the exit status of a successful command?
questions.why: Non-zero values mean some kind of failure.

questions.q: What does && do between two commands?
options: Runs the second only if the first succeeds
Runs the second only if the first fails
questions.why: make && make install installs only if the build worked.

questions.q: What does ; do between commands?
options: Runs the second only on success
Runs them one after another regardless of success
questions.why: cmd1; cmd2 always runs both, whether or not the first one succeeds.

questions.q: What does an if statement test in bash?
options: The exit status of a command
questions.why: if grep -q x file; then ... runs the block when grep succeeds.

questions.q: Which test checks whether a file exists and is a regular file?
questions.why: -d tests for a directory and -x for executable.

questions.q: Which test checks whether a string is empty?
questions.why: -z is true for a zero-length string; -n for non-empty.

questions.q: Which operator compares integers for 'greater than' in [ ]?
questions.why: Inside [ ], > is a redirection, so integer tests use -gt, -lt, -eq and so on.

questions.q: What does a case statement do in bash?
options: Matches a value against patterns and runs the matching block
questions.why: It's cleaner than many if/elif tests for one variable.

questions.q: How do you define a function in bash?
questions.why: Functions keep repeated code in one place.

questions.q: What does $1 mean inside a script?
options: The first argument passed to the script
questions.why: $0 is the script name and $# the argument count.

questions.q: What does "$@" expand to?
options: All arguments, each as a separate quoted word
questions.why: Quoted $@ preserves arguments that contain spaces.

questions.q: What does set -e do at the top of a script?
options: Exits the script as soon as a command fails
questions.why: It stops scripts carrying on after errors.

questions.q: What does bash -x script.sh do?
options: Runs the script, printing each command before it runs
questions.why: Tracing prints each command as it runs, which makes scripts easier to debug.

questions.q: What does a here document (<<EOF) do?
options: Feeds a block of text to a command's standard input
questions.why: Useful for writing multi-line config into files from a script.

questions.q: What does crontab's 0 2 * * * field pattern mean?
options: Run on the 2nd of each month
questions.why: The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week.

questions.q: What does */15 in a crontab minute field mean?
questions.why: */15 matches minutes 0, 15, 30 and 45 of every hour.

questions.q: Where are system-wide cron jobs often placed?
questions.why: Directories like /etc/cron.daily run scripts on a schedule too.

questions.q: What does systemctl status sshd show?
options: Whether the service is running, plus recent log lines
questions.why: It's the first check when a service misbehaves.

questions.q: Which command starts a service now and enables it at boot?
questions.why: enable alone only affects boot; --now also starts it.

questions.q: Which command shows logs for a specific systemd service?
questions.why: journalctl -u sshd shows that unit's logs; add -f to follow new lines.

questions.q: What does dmesg show?
options: Kernel ring buffer messages such as hardware and driver events
questions.why: dmesg helps diagnose disk, USB and driver problems.

questions.q: Where are most traditional log files kept?
questions.why: Systems with persistent journald also keep logs in /var/log/journal.

questions.q: What does logrotate do?
options: Rotates, compresses and deletes old log files on a schedule
questions.why: Rotating and compressing old logs stops them from filling the disk.

questions.q: What does the ping command test?
options: Whether a host is reachable over the network
questions.why: ping sends ICMP echo requests and reports replies and timing.

questions.q: Which command shows the route packets take to a host on Linux?
questions.why: traceroute lists each router hop between you and the destination.

questions.q: Which command looks up DNS records with detailed output?
questions.why: dig example.com MX shows the MX records and the server that answered.

questions.q: Which file sets the DNS servers a Linux system uses?
questions.why: On many modern systems it's managed by NetworkManager or systemd-resolved.

questions.q: What is /etc/hosts used for?
options: Static name-to-IP mappings checked before DNS
questions.why: It's handy for testing or small networks.

questions.q: Which command shows or sets the hostname on systemd systems?
questions.why: hostnamectl set-hostname name changes it persistently.

questions.q: What does ssh-keygen do?
options: Creates a public/private key pair for SSH
questions.why: The private key stays on your machine; the public key goes to servers.

questions.q: What does ssh-copy-id do?
options: Installs your public key in a remote account's authorized_keys
questions.why: Afterwards you can log in with the key instead of a password.

questions.q: Which command copies files securely between hosts?
questions.why: Both scp and sftp run over SSH, so files and passwords are encrypted.

questions.q: What does rsync -avz src/ host:dest/ do?
options: Syncs files to a remote host with archive mode, verbose output and compression
questions.why: rsync copies only changes, making repeat transfers fast.

questions.q: What does curl -I https://example.com show?
questions.why: -I sends a HEAD request, so only the response headers come back.

questions.q: What does wget do?
questions.why: wget downloads files from the web; wget -c resumes an interrupted download.

questions.q: What package manager do Debian and Ubuntu use?
questions.why: apt install package installs software with dependencies.

questions.q: What package manager do RHEL and Fedora use?
questions.why: dnf replaced yum and resolves dependencies automatically.

questions.q: Which command lists installed packages on an RPM-based system?
questions.why: -q means query and -a means all packages, so rpm -qa lists everything installed.

questions.q: Which command shows which package owns a file on an RPM system?
questions.why: rpm -ql lists the files a package installed.

questions.q: Which command shows which package owns a file on Debian?
questions.why: dpkg -L package lists the files it installed.

questions.q: What does apt update do?
options: Refreshes the list of available packages
questions.why: apt upgrade then installs newer versions.

questions.q: What is a shebang line?
options: The first line, like #!/bin/bash, naming the script's interpreter
questions.why: Without it, the script runs in whatever shell launched it.

questions.q: What does uname -r show?
questions.why: uname -r prints the running kernel release; uname -a shows everything.

questions.q: Which file usually identifies the Linux distribution and version?
questions.why: Scripts read os-release to detect the distribution.

questions.q: What does lsmod list?
questions.why: modprobe loads modules and rmmod removes them.

questions.q: What does lsof show?
options: Open files and the processes using them
questions.why: lsof lists open files and their processes; lsof -i adds network sockets.

questions.q: What does the screen or tmux command provide?
options: Terminal sessions that keep running after you disconnect
questions.why: Long jobs over SSH survive a dropped connection.

questions.q: What does shutdown -r now do?
questions.why: shutdown -h now halts; systemctl reboot also restarts.

questions.q: Which directory holds essential user command binaries in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard?
questions.why: On modern distributions /bin is usually a symbolic link to /usr/bin, where the commands actually live.

questions.q: Which directory holds variable data such as logs, mail spools and caches?
questions.why: Data in /var changes as the system runs, so it's often a separate filesystem on servers.

questions.q: Which directory is meant for optional add-on software packages?
questions.why: Third-party applications often install themselves under /opt/<vendor>.

questions.q: Which directory holds temporary files that may be cleared at reboot?
questions.why: Anyone can write to /tmp, which is why the sticky bit protects other users' files there.

questions.q: What is /proc?
options: A virtual filesystem exposing kernel and process information
questions.why: Files under /proc are generated by the kernel on demand and take no disk space.

questions.q: What is /sys used for?
options: A virtual filesystem exposing devices and kernel settings
questions.why: sysfs lets tools read and change device and driver settings.

questions.q: Which directory holds the home directory of the root user?
questions.why: Root's home is separate so it stays available even if /home is on a failed disk.

questions.q: What is /srv intended for?
options: Data served by the system, such as web or FTP content
questions.why: Some admins keep website files under /srv instead of /var/www.

questions.q: What is an inode?
options: A data structure holding a file's metadata and data locations
questions.why: File names live in directories and point to inodes, which hold permissions, owner, size and block pointers.

questions.q: Which command shows a file's inode number?
questions.why: Hard links to the same file share an inode number, which ls -i reveals.

questions.q: Why can't hard links point to directories in normal use?
options: It could create loops in the filesystem tree
questions.why: Allowing directory hard links would let the tree contain cycles that confuse tools like find.

questions.q: What happens to a hard-linked file's data when one of its names is deleted?
options: The data stays until the last link is removed
questions.why: The inode tracks a link count, and the data is freed only when that count reaches zero.

questions.q: What happens to a symbolic link when its target is deleted?
options: It keeps a copy of the data
questions.why: A symlink only stores a path; if nothing exists at that path, the link is broken.

questions.q: What are the three standard file descriptors?
questions.why: Redirection uses these numbers, as in 2> for errors.

questions.q: What does 2>&1 mean?
options: Send standard error to wherever standard output is going
questions.why: command > out.txt 2>&1 puts both streams in out.txt; the order of the redirections matters.

questions.q: What is /dev/null?
options: A special file that discards anything written to it
questions.why: command > /dev/null 2>&1 silences all output from a command.

questions.q: What does the xargs command do?
options: Builds command lines from standard input
questions.why: find . -name '*.log' | xargs rm passes the found names to rm as arguments.

questions.q: What does the cut -c1-5 command do?
options: Prints characters 1 to 5 of each line
questions.why: -c selects by character position and -f by field.

questions.q: What does wc -l < file print compared with wc -l file?
options: Just the number, without the file name
questions.why: When input comes from redirection, wc doesn't know a file name, so it prints only the count.

questions.q: What does the column -t command do?
options: Formats whitespace-separated text into aligned columns
questions.why: It makes messy output, like mount or a CSV with -s,, easier to read.

questions.q: What does nl -ba file do?
options: Numbers every line, including blank ones
questions.why: nl's default numbers only non-blank lines, so -ba changes that.

questions.q: What does fold -w 40 do?
questions.why: Use -s to break at spaces so words aren't split.

questions.q: What does split -l 1000 big.txt part_ do?
options: Splits big.txt into files of 1,000 lines each named part_aa, part_ab and so on
questions.why: cat part_* > big.txt joins them back together.

questions.q: In a regular expression, what does ^ mean at the start of a pattern?
options: Match at the beginning of a line
Match the end of a line
questions.why: grep '^root' finds lines that start with root.

questions.q: In a regular expression, what does $ mean at the end of a pattern?
options: Match at the end of a line
questions.why: grep 'bash$' finds lines ending in bash.

questions.q: In a regular expression, what does . match?
questions.why: Use \. to match an actual dot, such as in an IP address.

questions.q: In extended regex, what does + mean?
options: One or more of the previous item
questions.why: grep -E '[0-9]+' matches one or more digits.

questions.q: What does [^0-9] match?
options: Any single character that is not a digit
A line starting with a digit
questions.why: A ^ inside square brackets negates the set, so this matches any non-digit.

questions.q: What does sed -n '5,10p' file do?
questions.why: -n suppresses normal output so only the p-printed lines appear.

questions.q: What does sed '/^#/d' file do?
options: Deletes lines starting with #, showing the rest
questions.why: This is a quick way to view a config file without its comment lines.

questions.q: What does sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' file do?
options: Edits the file in place and keeps a backup named file.bak
Creates a new file named b
questions.why: On BSD and macOS sed, -i requires the backup suffix argument.

questions.q: What does awk 'NR==3' file print?
questions.why: NR is the current line number, so the pattern matches only line 3.

questions.q: What does awk '{print NF}' file print?
options: The number of fields on each line
questions.why: Use $NF to print the last field's value instead.

questions.q: What does awk '$3 > 100' file print?
options: Lines whose third field is greater than 100
questions.why: A pattern with no action prints matching lines by default.

questions.q: What does the tr -d '\r' command do?
options: Removes carriage return characters, such as from Windows text files
questions.why: Windows line endings cause odd errors in Linux scripts until the \r is removed.

questions.q: What is the default runlevel equivalent for a server without a GUI on systemd?
questions.why: graphical.target adds the display manager on top of multi-user.target.

questions.q: Which command changes the system to rescue mode right now?
questions.why: isolate starts the target and stops units it doesn't need.

questions.q: What is a systemd unit file?
options: A configuration file describing a service, mount, timer or other unit
questions.why: Unit files live in /usr/lib/systemd/system, with local overrides in /etc/systemd/system.

questions.q: Where should you put custom or overriding systemd unit files?
questions.why: Files in /etc take priority over the vendor copies and survive package updates.

questions.q: What must you run after editing a systemd unit file?
questions.why: daemon-reload makes systemd re-read unit files before you restart the service.

questions.q: What is a systemd timer?
options: A unit that runs a service on a schedule, like cron
questions.why: systemctl list-timers shows timers and when they will run next.

questions.q: What does systemctl list-units --failed show?
questions.why: It's a quick health check after boot or changes.

questions.q: What does systemctl mask do to a service?
options: Prevents it from being started at all, even manually or as a dependency
questions.why: Masking links the unit to /dev/null; systemctl unmask reverses it.

questions.q: What is the first program the kernel runs at boot on most modern Linux systems?
questions.why: PID 1 starts and supervises every other service.

questions.q: What is GRUB?
options: The boot loader that loads the kernel
questions.why: GRUB shows the boot menu and passes kernel parameters.

questions.q: What is the initramfs (initial RAM filesystem)?
options: A small temporary root filesystem with drivers needed to mount the real root
questions.why: It lets the kernel reach root filesystems on RAID, LVM or encrypted disks.

questions.q: How can you pass a one-time kernel parameter at boot?
options: Edit the GRUB entry at the boot menu by pressing e
questions.why: Changes made at the menu apply to that boot only.

questions.q: Which command makes permanent changes to kernel boot arguments on RHEL?
questions.why: grubby edits the boot loader entries so the arguments persist.

questions.q: What does sysctl do?
options: Views and changes kernel parameters at runtime
questions.why: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 enables IP forwarding until reboot.

questions.q: How do you make a sysctl setting permanent?
options: Put it in a file under /etc/sysctl.d/ and run sysctl --system
questions.why: Files in /etc/sysctl.d/ are applied at every boot.

questions.q: Which command lists PCI devices?
questions.why: lspci -k also shows which kernel driver each device uses.

questions.q: Which command lists USB devices?
questions.why: It helps confirm whether a plugged-in device was detected.

questions.q: Which command shows CPU details such as cores and architecture?
questions.why: lscpu summarises information from /proc/cpuinfo.

questions.q: What does modprobe do?
options: Loads a kernel module along with its dependencies
questions.why: modprobe -r removes a module and unused dependencies.

questions.q: What does SELinux's getenforce show?
options: The current mode: Enforcing, Permissive or Disabled
questions.why: setenforce switches between enforcing and permissive until reboot.

questions.q: What does SELinux permissive mode do?
options: Logs policy violations but doesn't block them
questions.why: Permissive mode is useful for troubleshooting without turning SELinux off.

questions.q: Which ls option shows SELinux security contexts?
questions.why: Contexts look like system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0.

questions.q: Which command restores default SELinux contexts on files?
questions.why: restorecon -Rv /path applies the contexts defined in policy.

questions.q: What is an SELinux boolean?
options: An on/off switch that adjusts policy for common needs
questions.why: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on allows web apps to make network connections.

questions.q: Which tool manages the firewall on RHEL and Fedora?
questions.why: firewall-cmd --permanent changes rules that survive a reload.

questions.q: Which tool is the simple firewall front end on Ubuntu?
questions.why: ufw allow 22/tcp opens SSH; ufw enable turns the firewall on.

questions.q: What does firewall-cmd --reload do?
options: Applies permanent rules to the running firewall
questions.why: Rules added with --permanent take effect only after a reload.

questions.q: What is a firewalld zone?
options: A named set of rules applied to interfaces or sources based on trust
questions.why: Common zones include public, internal and trusted.

questions.q: Which command shows listening TCP and UDP ports with process names?
questions.why: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening, -p processes and -n numeric output.

questions.q: Which command adds a temporary IP address to an interface?
questions.why: Changes made with ip disappear at reboot unless saved in the network configuration.

questions.q: Which command adds a default route temporarily?
questions.why: To keep it, configure the gateway with NetworkManager or the distro's network files.

questions.q: Which command lists NetworkManager connections?
questions.why: nmcli con mod and nmcli con up change and activate connections.

questions.q: What does ip link set eth0 down do?
questions.why: The interface stops passing traffic; ip link set eth0 up brings it back.

questions.q: What does the date command with +%F print?
questions.why: Format codes like %H:%M show hours and minutes; %s shows Unix time.

questions.q: Which command sets the time zone on systemd systems?
questions.why: timedatectl also shows whether the clock is synchronised.

questions.q: What is chrony?
options: An NTP client and server for keeping time accurate
questions.why: chronyc sources shows which time servers it is using.

questions.q: What does the at command do differently from cron?
options: Runs a job once at a set time rather than repeatedly
questions.why: atq lists pending jobs and atrm removes them.

questions.q: What does the watch command do?
options: Runs a command repeatedly and shows its output full screen
questions.why: watch -n 5 df -h refreshes disk usage every 5 seconds.

questions.q: What does nohup do?
options: Lets a command keep running after you log out
questions.why: Output goes to nohup.out unless you redirect it.

questions.q: What does the time command report?
options: How long a command took to run, including CPU time
questions.why: real is wall-clock time; user and sys are CPU time.

questions.q: What does stat -c %s file print?
questions.why: stat -c accepts format codes for any file attribute.

questions.q: What does the basename command do?
options: Strips the directory part from a path, leaving the file name
questions.why: basename /var/log/syslog prints syslog; dirname prints /var/log.

questions.q: What does readlink -f do?
options: Prints the full resolved path, following all symlinks
questions.why: It's useful in scripts that need a script's real location.

questions.q: What does mktemp create?
options: A temporary file or directory with a unique, unpredictable name
questions.why: Safe temp names avoid race-condition attacks in shared /tmp.

questions.q: What does the umask command with no arguments show?
questions.why: umask -S shows it in symbolic form, such as u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx.

questions.q: What is a process's niceness?
options: A value that influences its scheduling priority
questions.why: Higher niceness means the process yields CPU to others more readily.

questions.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
options: Threads share their process's memory; separate processes have their own
questions.why: Threads are lighter weight but a bug in one can affect the whole process.

questions.q: What is a daemon?
questions.why: Daemon names often end in d, like sshd and crond.

questions.q: What does the D state mean in ps or top output?
options: Uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on I/O
questions.why: Many D-state processes often point to slow or failing storage.

questions.q: What does the R state mean in ps output?
questions.why: S means sleeping, T stopped and Z zombie.

questions.q: What does pstree show?
options: Processes as a tree of parents and children
questions.why: It makes it easy to see which process started which.

questions.q: What does the kill -l command show?
options: The list of signal names and numbers
questions.why: Signals include SIGHUP 1, SIGINT 2, SIGKILL 9 and SIGTERM 15.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+C send to the foreground process?
questions.why: Programs can catch SIGINT to clean up before exiting.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+D do at an empty shell prompt?
options: Sends end-of-file, which logs out of the shell
questions.why: In programs reading input, it signals the end of input.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the /etc/skel directory?
options: Template files copied into new users' home directories
questions.why: Put default .bashrc settings there so every new user gets them.

questions.q: What does useradd -s /bin/zsh alice do?
options: Creates alice with zsh as her login shell
questions.why: chsh -s changes an existing user's shell.

questions.q: What does usermod -L alice do?
options: Locks alice's password so she can't log in with it
questions.why: -L puts a ! before the password hash; usermod -U unlocks the account.

questions.q: What does gpasswd -d bob devs do?
options: Removes bob from the devs group
questions.why: -d removes a user from a group, and gpasswd -a adds one.

questions.q: What does newgrp do?
options: Starts a shell with a different primary group for the session
questions.why: Files you create then belong to that group.

questions.q: What does the last command read?
options: The wtmp log of logins and reboots
questions.why: last reads the wtmp log of logins and reboots; lastb shows failed logins.

questions.q: What does the w command add beyond who?
options: What each user is currently doing, plus load and idle times
questions.why: It's a quick view of who is on the system and what they run.

questions.q: What does the write or wall command do?
options: Sends a message to other users' terminals
questions.why: wall broadcasts to everyone, such as before a reboot.

questions.q: Which file contains the message shown after login on many systems?
questions.why: /etc/issue is shown before login on the console.

questions.q: What does tar's -p option do when extracting?
